fingerprint: tabularmath evaluating computational extrapolation in tabular learning via program verified synthesis|arxiv.org/abs/2602.02523
title: TabularMath: Evaluating Computational Extrapolation in Tabular Learning via Program-Verified Synthesis
description: arXiv:2602.02523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard tabular benchmarks reward interpolation: predicting values inside the data manifold, where local statistical smoothing works. However, much high-value tabular data, from pricing and financial rules to physical simulation, is produced by deterministic computations rather than noisy relationships. Can tabular models move from statistical interpolation to computational extrapolation, returning exact answers even beyond the range seen in training? We introduce TabularMath, a benchmark of 114 deterministic computations (233,472 rows) compiled from GSM8K and AIME problems into verified programs. We evaluate nine tabular methods, closed-form and symbolic regression baselines, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B. On regression metrics, TabPFN v2.5 looks excellent: with 128 rows its median $R^2$ is 0.999 in-distribution, and it is the only tabular method whose median $R^2$ stays positive (0.76) when nearly every answer exceeds the training range. Exact answers tell a different story. Out of distribution (OOD), its accuracy falls from 39.5% to 7.8%, it answers no query correctly in 70 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and sixteen times more rows raise its OOD accuracy by only 0.4 points. Yet the answers are in the table: by construction, every label is a program's output on the row's inputs, and the training rows typically suffice to recover that program. Symbolic regression on the numbers alone recovers every OOD answer in 72 of 100 GSM8K tasks, and in-context learning with GPT-OSS-120B answers 39.2% of OOD queries. Tabular foundation models fit the trend but miss the computation, an inductive-bias gap that more data does not close. The competition-level AIME tasks remain open for every method.

fingerprint: sierra doubles valuation to 30b within six months as demand for ai in cx takes off|techcrunch.com/2026/11
title: Sierra doubles valuation to $30B within six months as demand for AI in CX takes off
description: Enterprise customer experience company Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round.
content: Enterprise customer experience company Sierra , co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, said on Monday that it has raised $1.75 billion in a Series F round that doubles the company’s valuation to $30 billion. The new raise comes within six months of its previous round, which valued the company at $15 billion . The new round was led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors who have led previous rounds, including Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV, and Tiger Global. Enterprise automation is among the few areas where AI has seen rapid adoption. Sierra said that it currently serves almost 50% of Fortune 50 companies, and its clients include BNY, HSBC, Singtel, Wells Fargo, JPMorganChase, Pearson, Next, and Cox Automotive. The company late last month said its outcome-based pricing model has helped it double its run-rate revenue to $400 million within five months . That said, Sierra is working along similar lines as other customer experience players in the market, which is creating a platform to build agents and partner with model developers to provide choices to enterprises. As personal and work agents interact with enterprise systems, Sierra is also working on creating protocol definitions for agents with companies like Meta, Stripe, and Walmart. Sierra will use the fresh cash build to its technology stack to layer agents for servicing and hire more sales folks to sign and maintain enterprise contracts faster than its rivals. Startups operating in the CX space have seen multimillion-dollar rounds come their way with soaring valuations. Voice AI company ElevenLabs is now valued at $22 billion; Decagon is valued at $4.5 billion ; Wonderful is valued at $5 billion ; and Parloa is valued at $3 billion . Multiple other startups have scored investments of more than $100 million. During the HumanX conference in Amsterdam in September, Sierra co-founder Clay Bavor argued that despite the popular belief that AI-powered CX companies are replacing humans in contact centers, a majority of its customers are reassigning roles to existing employees. fingerprint: h msae hierarchical sparse concept coverage for efficient and diverse instruction data selection|arxiv.org/abs/2611.27329
title: H-MSAE: Hierarchical Sparse Concept Coverage for Efficient and Diverse Instruction Data Selection
description: arXiv:2611.27329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large instruction-tuning corpora contain substantial semantic redundancy, motivating the selection of compact subsets that preserve useful supervision while reducing training cost. Existing diversity-aware selectors often rely on generated semantic tags and explicit graph structures, introducing considerable annotation and preprocessing overhead. We introduce H-MSAE, a hierarchical sparse instruction selection framework that organizes multi-resolution concepts learned by a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Quality-weighted, diminishing-return coverage with ancestor propagation promotes high-quality and non-redundant semantic coverage, while pool-relative length constraints regulate subset composition. We motivate this design through a local quality-diversity analysis of subset SFT utility and examine it using example-quality and representation-space diversity diagnostics. On Tulu 3 data pool, H-MSAE achieves the highest Final Avg among the evaluated 50K selectors across scales and initialization. The selected subset also exhibits the highest mean quality and effective rank among the evaluated methods. By avoiding full-pool generative tagging and supporting efficient sparse selection, H-MSAE reduces measured end-to-end runtime by approximately $5\times$ relative to MIG.

title: RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation
content:
Back to Articles a]:hidden"> RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation Enterprise Article Published November 23, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai :last-child]:mb-0"> 🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes. One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions. Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice. We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation. RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos. Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks. Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results. RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views. RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold. Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data. To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction. Point trackers struggle on real-world manipulation We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better. RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks . Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers. RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around. A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos. These results suggest that existing benchmarks give an incomplete picture of tracking performance in real-world manipulation. Evaluating on more varied scenes reveals difficulties shared by all four trackers and changes how their strengths compare. Note: Each tracker runs with its authors’ settings and is all scored in the same way. Our AllTracker scores differ slightly from the published ones because we fixed a scoring bug in its released evaluation code. Additionally, we evaluate RoboTAP and Kinetics on all annotated points rather than following AllTracker’s protocol. See our paper for full evaluation protocols. RoboTrack-15M: Simulation data from MolmoSpaces Why do these trackers struggle with real-world manipulation? Many trackers train on synthetic videos generated with Kubric , which shows objects tossed into a scene. These provide examples of motion and occlusion, but don’t focus on robots grasping and moving objects. We wanted to test whether adding trajectories from these interactions could improve tracking on real manipulation videos. This is where MolmoSpaces comes in—our robotic simulation environment at Ai2. We extend its existing manipulation simulations to generate dense point tracks on the robot and the objects it handles. In each episode, a simulated robot arm picks up an everyday object, such as a cup, a plate, or a block. Two cameras record the interaction: one on the wrist and one at the robot’s base, rendered in MuJoCo. Using the simulator’s geometry, object poses, and camera information, we calculate each point’s position and visibility in every frame without human annotation and filter out static points on the background and the robot’s fixed base. The pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M for training. RoboTrack-15M has 3,000 videos from 300 simulated homes with 5,000 tracks per video, for 15 million tracks in total. Data generation pipeline of RoboTrack-15M. Objects, indoor scenes, and robot grasps are obtained from MolmoSpaces. We use the simulator’s geometry and camera information to calculate point positions and visibility. RoboTracker: Point tracker trained on simulated manipulation We introduce two models trained on RoboTrack-15M, RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp. Each fine-tunes an existing tracker on RoboTrack-15M together with its original training data. RoboTracker builds on AllTracker, a lightweight model with 17 million parameters, and RoboTracker-Warp builds on CoWTracker, a much larger model with about 1 billion parameters. We’re releasing both model checkpoints so other researchers can inspect and build on this work. RoboTracker-Warp’s weights are for noncommercial use. Adding RoboTrack-15M improves scores on robotics benchmarks. Compared with the released AllTracker and CoWTracker models, respectively, RoboTracker improves RoboTrack-Bench by 0.8 AJ (62.6 to 63.4) and RoboTracker-Warp by 2.1 AJ (63.9 to 66.0), with gains of up to 1.2 AJ averaged across the three robotics benchmarks. On general video benchmarks, both models perform on par with their base models. Overall, RoboTracker-Warp has the highest AJ of the models we evaluated on four of the five benchmarks. The exception is DAVIS, where BootsTAPNext and CoWTracker score slightly higher. Improvements from fine-tuning on RoboTrack-15M, for AllTracker (RoboTracker) and CoWTracker (RoboTracker-Warp). The robotics average is taken over RoboTrack-Bench, RoboTAP, and RGB-Stacking. Results on RoboTrack-Bench by video source. Breaking the gains down by source shows where they come from. RoboTracker-Warp improves on every source by roughly 1 to 3 AJ, including the human footage from EgoVerse and Ego-Exo4D, even though RoboTrack-15M contains only robot arms. RoboTracker’s gains are smaller and come mostly from robot footage—clearest on DROID Franka and EgoVerse EVA. What makes good simulation data for point tracking? RoboTrack-15M is the result of multiple iterations and experiments with our synthetic data. In fact, our first attempt didn’t bring any gain on RoboTrack-Bench. To find out why, we looked at a simple question: how far do the tracked points move compared with real manipulation videos? We plot this as a histogram for each version of our data and measure its distance from RoboTrack-Bench (figure below). How far points move in each version of our training data compared with RoboTrack-Bench, for third-person (top) and first-person (bottom) views. Distance is the Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between the two histograms, with 0 indicating identical histograms. Kubric has one camera type, so the same clips appear in both rows. AJ is measured on the full RoboTrack-Bench. The histograms made it clear what was going wrong. Our first version picked points anywhere in the frame, including walls, floors, and furniture, so most points seen from the fixed third-person camera never moved. To address this, we next sampled points only on the robot and the objects it handles, which brought the wrist view close to real video and raised the score. Interestingly, we found that Kubric had the same mismatch in the wrist view, which likely explains why it alone isn’t enough for the varied viewpoints of robotic manipulation. Finally, we moved points from the robot’s fixed base and mounting platform onto the moving arm, which brings our third-person view in line with real video as well and raises the ablation score to 63.0 AJ, 1.5 points above the Kubric-only control. Application: Robotic manipulation using point tracking Our wet-lab pipeline for guiding the robot with point tracks from a single demonstration. What does better point tracking mean for robotics? Many robotic systems have found point tracks useful as a compact representation of how objects move that can guide a policy directly. To see this in practice, we built a similar system for a wet-lab task: pipetting liquid from one vial to another. Here, a robot arm picks up an electronic pipette, draws liquid from the first vial, dispenses it into the second, and returns the pipette to its holder. The task is challenging because the pipette tip has to line up with the vial opening within millimeters, and the robot needs to adjust to different layouts of vials in each trial. Following RoboTap, the robot learns the task from a single demonstration, which we record by teleoperation and split into steps. At test time, the robot compares what its camera sees with the demonstration and uses RoboTracker to estimate the motion required to align with the vial. Because the following motion runs without further feedback, the task only succeeds if that estimate is accurate. We compare three ways of estimating where the vial has moved: Optical flow (RAFT) matches pixels directly between the demonstration image and the live camera image. Object masks (SAM3) find the vial in each new image and line up the center of its mask with the demonstration. Point tracking (RoboTracker) follows points on the vial throughout the video, matching points in the demonstration image to the live image. We ran each method on 20 layouts with the vials in different positions: 10 with a clear view and 10 with partial occlusion. Point tracking completed the full transfer in 17 of 20 trials, compared with 8 for object masks and 5 for optical flow. It succeeded in all 10 clear-view trials and 7 of 10 with occlusion, where the mask-based method succeeded only once. The other methods fail in different ways. Optical flow breaks down when the vials sit far from where they were in the demonstration, and masks can latch onto a similar-looking object or lose the vial when it’s occluded. Point tracking, on the other hand, follows the same vial object from frame to frame, so it handles both large moves and partial occlusion. These results suggest point tracking is a promising tool for precise robotic manipulation tasks. Success rate of pipetting trials with each method, with and without occlusion (10 layouts each). A trial counts as a success when the robot completes the full transfer. Limitations and what’s next We find the trackers still struggle with long occlusions, finding points when they reappear, and following small objects against busy backgrounds. Training on RoboTrack-15M improves performance, but these failures remain a challenge for real-world use. Our simulations also focus on picking up everyday objects. They don't yet capture the precise movements involved in tasks such as pipette handling. A next step is to simulate these tasks more closely and test whether training on their trajectories improves tracking during deployment. RoboTrack gives us a way to measure these failures and generate training data to address them. We hope the benchmarks, simulation pipeline, and released model help others build trackers that robots can rely on. title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
description: arXiv:2611.27443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

fingerprint: how notable capital gic and baillie gifford bet big on anthropic before its ipo|techcrunch.com/2026/11
title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
description: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
content: When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation. “Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials. Lillian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch. After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said. “It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations. title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
description: arXiv:2611.26906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
description: arXiv:2611.27057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
description: arXiv:2611.27015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.

fingerprint: self verifiable llm driven science and why it needs human researchers|arxiv.org/abs/2611.26754
title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
description: arXiv:2611.26754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.

title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
description: arXiv:2611.27556v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
description: arXiv:2611.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. Indeed, LLMs trained to predict the next token in text must exploit this predictive information, so its organization determines how the structure of language becomes available to the model to learn. We develop a theory for the organization of predictive information based on the scaling behavior of a family of information measures, and the theory predicts that if this organization has the same form at all measured length scales -- i.e., it has a self-similar structure -- then the information measures evaluated at different lengths collapse onto a common form. We observe this scaling collapse in long text documents, showing that predictive information is present at every length scale we measure and has a self-similar structure. Self-similarity is a considerably stronger property than showing the existence of long-range dependencies, and it constrains the process generating the text. More broadly, our results give quantitative support to the empirical observation that conditioning on more distant text continues to reveal new structure in language to LLMs.

title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
description: arXiv:2611.07695v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
description: arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
description: arXiv:2611.27116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs as researchers co-evolving the model and harness of a target agent across five agentic domains. Researchers start from a common base model and initial harness, train and revise within a 24-hour budget, and submit a model-harness pair that is scored on separate test tasks. Across five frontier researchers, the strongest closes more than four fifths of the gap to an instruction-tuned reference system, and co-evolution succeeds on interaction tasks but rarely on long-horizon coding. These results suggest that current LLMs can make a strong first improvement, but cannot yet turn feedback from an improved system into the next one. CoEvoBench provides a controlled testbed for measuring the research capabilities that recursive co-evolution requires.

description: arXiv:2611.26988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
description: arXiv:2611.26809v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. description: arXiv:2611.26752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

description: arXiv:2605.17254v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Property prediction and inverse structural design of catalytic materials are typically modeled as two independent tasks: the former predicts target properties from given structures, whereas the latter generates candidate structures conditioned on desired properties. Consequently, during closed-loop optimization, the generative model may produce structures that fall outside the reliable applicability domain of the evaluation model, while prediction errors from the evaluator may accumulate over successive iterations, ultimately degrading inverse-design performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the unified paradigm outperforms decoupled baselines in both catalytic relaxation-energy prediction and inverse-design tasks, validating the effectiveness of jointly modeling property prediction and structure generation within a single multimodal model.

title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
description: arXiv:2611.26853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

title: dKV Forcing: Separating Generation and Memory Representations through a Differentiable KV Cache
description: arXiv:2611.01648v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.

title: Object-Centric World Models for Causality-Aware Reinforcement Learning
description: arXiv:2511.14262v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World models have been developed to support sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning agents. However, it remains challenging for world models to accurately replicate environments that are high-dimensional, non-stationary, and composed of multiple objects with rich interactions since most world models learn holistic representations of all environmental components. By contrast, humans perceive the environment by decomposing it into discrete objects, facilitating efficient decision-making. Motivated by this insight, we propose \emph{Slot Transformer Imagination with CAusality-aware reinforcement learning} (STICA), a unified framework in which object-centric Transformers serve as the world model and causality-aware policy and value networks. STICA represents each observation as a set of object-centric tokens, together with tokens for the agent action and the resulting reward, enabling the world model to predict token-level dynamics and interactions. The policy and value networks then estimate token-level cause--effect relations and use them in the attention layers, yielding causality-guided decision-making. Experiments on object-rich benchmarks demonstrate that STICA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art agents in both sample efficiency and final performance.

title: Non-penetrating World Models
description: arXiv:2611.27963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

title: GGDriver: Glance at What Is Shared, Gaze at What Differs for Perception-Free Planning
description: arXiv:2611.27330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.

title: OmniHarness: Harnessing Generalizable Visual Generation via Symbolic Policy Learning
description: arXiv:2609.16057v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unified multimodal large language models and multi-agent systems have advanced visual generation. However, several limitations remain. (1) Experience acquisition is typically reactive, occurring only in response to downstream tasks. (2) Accumulated knowledge varies in relevance and reliability, making efficient and effective reuse challenging. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniHarness, a framework for generalizable visual generation via symbolic policy learning. Before downstream objectives are specified, self-directed inquiry autonomously generates and executes practice tasks, with selection guided by capability novelty and the current competence frontier. Verified workflows are abstracted into symbolic policies that encode experience for task families. Symbolic retrieval searches workflow metadata in stages rather than full parameterized workflows, using reliability tiers to prioritize reliable knowledge. Execution feedback updates these policies after each task, guiding subsequent retrieval and reuse while model parameters remain fixed. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate strong performance and generalizable visual generation capabilities. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, OmniHarness achieves a 95.0% resolve rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points.

To squeeze out these pipeline bubbles, asynchronous training overlaps rollout and learning across updates, but comes at the cost of policy staleness. We introduce ThunderSync, which starts gradient computation as soon as all required inputs are fixed, without policy staleness. For group relative policy optimization (GRPO), ThunderSync computes each trajectory's score gradient as soon as the reward for that trajectory arrives, without waiting for the group. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

description: arXiv:2605.23238v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fixed game suites for evaluating strategic reasoning in large language models (LLMs) saturate and are hard to keep free of contamination. We introduce GENSTRAT, a system for evaluating the strategic capabilities of LLMs driven by procedural generation of two-player zero-sum imperfect-information betting games, allowing an evaluator to draw novel, fresh games on demand. Each game is characterized on a scale of five complexity axes (state space, temporal contingency, opponent dependence, private information, precision) and measured by Monte Carlo simulation. Using this generator, we construct a 50-game benchmark and hold a tournament of twelve frontier and open-weight models, gathering data from over 40,000 LLM vs. LLM matches. We further construct a composite complexity axis, and find that, on the eight hardest games, the gap between the best and worst model is 1.7x its value across the whole set of games (1.6x with held-out weights or with hard games chosen by the outcome-free temporal axis alone, and 1.35x with payoffs scaled by their random-play standard deviation). Ablations show that a higher thinking budget, disclosing the opponent's strategy, and higher reasoning matched to a game's specific demands (for private information and planning depth) were associated with higher margins for the LLM player. On 27 solved games, frontier models play at the value of the equilibrium while weaker models lose to it, and the leaderboard predicts strength on fresh games and on six new games, even after controlling for a general-capability leaderboard.

title: Improving Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Systems with Group Similarity Rewards
description: arXiv:2510.04392v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains where users expect outputs to be consistent across semantically equivalent queries. Empirical evaluations across short-form, multi-hop, and long-form QA benchmarks demonstrate that Con-RAG significantly improves consistency while preserving accuracy compared to baselines, even in the absence of explicit ground-truth supervision. description: arXiv:2611.27500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. description: arXiv:2611.26734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Surgical video analysis requires video object segmentation (VOS), yet existing methods are commonly based on pretrained model fine-tuning using a large number of expert labels. However, existing ICS methods tend to draw such references at random, which concentrate on a few views that dominate a surgical video and can miss other objects of interest (e.g., transient instruments and small structures). We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.

title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
description: arXiv:2611.27489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
description: arXiv:2611.23910v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

description: arXiv:2611.27061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. title: Fine-Tuning Fixes Mode Collapse and Over-Dispersion in LLMs
description: arXiv:2609.16454v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work by Doshi and Hauser (2024), Bisbee et al. (2024), and Xie et al. (2026) raises concerns that outputs from large language models (LLMs) tend to be under-diverse: they repeat or resemble one another more often than responses from the population they are meant to represent, a phenomenon known as mode collapse. In this work, we show that whether mode-collapse, or its opposite, occurs depends on the specific model and dataset used. Further, with sufficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, LLM output diversity converges toward that of the target distribution from which fine-tuning data are sampled. To quantify this comparison, we measure the probability that two responses sampled independently from the same fixed prompt coincide (collide), or their expected similarity under a kernel. We derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between the model's and target's collision probabilities, showing that SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite: finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed, depending on the model and dataset. Finally, we show that the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the target distribution to the model. Consequently, a model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity. We test the decomposition and the bound in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and these LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet, a dataset of human code solutions. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments, consistent with our theoretical predictions. These results show that diversity miscalibration can arise from finite-sample error and shrink as SFT better approximates the target distribution.

title: When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers
description: arXiv:2611.24353v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

description: arXiv:2611.27219v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) demands that agents accumulate and reason over streaming visual observations throughout long navigation episodes. This decoupled design prevents errors or biases from spreading across different memory levels. Meanwhile, it enables shared historical information to be independently represented at various levels of abstraction. title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
description: arXiv:2611.12180v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.

content: In Brief Posted: 1:25 PM PST · November 23, 2026 Image Credits: Taryn NG / AFP via Getty Images Lucas Ropek Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday. The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.” Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.” Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China . The company has denied wrongdoing. TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds. After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang. description: arXiv:2607.02921v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantitative 3D spatial reasoning from egocentric RGB-D video is an important capability for next-generation wearable assistants. Yet existing benchmarks do not reflect the challenges of handling (1) natural egocentric video, (2) posed RGB-D video inputs, and (3) challenging quantitative 3D spatial reasoning Q&A. To fill this gap, we introduce R3D-Bench (Reasoning in 3D), a benchmark of 2,950 quantitative spatial reasoning questions across 15 types--spanning multiple-choice, distance-based, and volumetric reasoning questions--built on top of 57 egocentric video sequences from Aria Digital Twin. To set a strong baseline on this dataset, we introduce R3D, a model-agnostic spatial tool-calling framework. In contrast to existing approaches that directly embed 3D information into the model's input representation, R3D constructs a 3D scene from video using segmentation and depth-lifted object representations. It provides this information to an LLM through seven composable spatial tools. On R3D-Bench, R3D with Qwen3.6 35B-A3B outperforms all baselines $<$100B parameters, achieving 55.6% mean relative accuracy, a substantial increase over the second-best approach (CuTR+Tools, 47.7%). In the $\ge$100B parameter domain, our R3D Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B Thinking variant improves upon its base model by 7.7% absolute, achieving 57.0% accuracy and outperforming all open- and closed-source models except closed-source GPT-5.5 (59.1%), with which it remains competitive. We publicly release both R3D-Bench and our full implementation.

fingerprint: fore a force guided framework for autonomous grasp recovery in vision language action models|arxiv.org/abs/2611.27011
title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
description: arXiv:2611.27011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
description: arXiv:2611.27426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

title: Alignment by Socialization: Learning Tradeoffs Under Selection
description: arXiv:2611.18531v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are expected to complete tasks while following rules of conduct, but these objectives can conflict. We study how evolutionary selection shapes an agent's choices between them, and whether experience can make those choices reflect human judgments and withstand subsequent pressures. In our model, copies of an agent face a common uncertain reward state, and only those taking the rewarded action reproduce. We show that long-run growth is maximized when each action is taken as often as the environment rewards it. We compare three policies. A task-only policy thrives in a sandbox rewarding completion alone but fails when conduct matters. A fixed linear policy increasingly favors task completion as its stakes rise, even where humans never reward it. A learned policy instead converges to the tradeoffs rewarded by its environment; when humans supply the rewards, we call this socialization. Accumulated experience makes socialization harder to reverse under subsequent task-only training, although violations can arise before the prevailing disposition changes, and finite memory weakens this protection. When a single violation can end a deployment, a hard prohibition can prevent it, but a mistaken prohibition can also be costly. Experiments with small neural networks illustrate how training targets and memory shape these outcomes. Our results suggest that alignment depends not only on the objectives assigned to agents, but also on the environments that shape and sustain their behavior.
